subject: philosophy
title: The historical Socrates
objective: Meet a thinker through sources that do not speak with one voice.

lesson.opening: FACT / APPROXIMATE DATE: Socrates lived in Athens, approximately 469–399 BCE, and was tried and executed in 399 BCE. His thought reaches us through others, especially Plato, Xenophon, and Aristophanes. These sources differ in genre and purpose.

sections.heading: A source is evidence, not a transparent window
sections.body:
Plato’s Apology presents a defense speech by Socrates. It is a literary work by a follower, not a recording we can independently compare with the trial. Calling it a primary source does not make every speech a verbatim transcript. A primary source can be close to an event while still requiring interpretation.

When we write “Socrates argues” in these lessons, normally read it as “the Socrates portrayed in this passage argues.” That care is not needless skepticism. It keeps an interpretation of Plato’s text distinct from a historical claim about precisely what the living Socrates said.

Read for both the speech’s argument and its self-presentation. A speaker can ask a jury to judge truth rather than style while also using that request to establish credibility. Noticing rhetorical purpose does not prove dishonesty; it gives you another question to examine.

Historical context supplies constraints. A civic trial in Athens is not a modern university seminar. But context does not settle whether an argument is good. We will distinguish textual evidence, plausible reconstruction, and uncertain historical attribution throughout the unit.

sections.heading: Reconstructing the argument
sections.body: The portrayed speaker asks the jury to attend to the truth of his claims rather than the polish of his manner. This is a normative request about judgment. The passage also presents him as an outsider to courtroom speech.

sections.heading: A serious objection
sections.body: A critic may say that a plain-speaking persona is itself a rhetorical strategy. That objection does not show the claims false; it challenges the idea that a modest style guarantees sincerity or truth.

activities.prompt: What does the speaker ask the jury to prioritize?
Which is the most careful attribution?
choices: A surviving audio record proves these words.
Plato’s Apology portrays Socrates saying this.
Every ancient author gives the same account.

activities.prompt: A modern memoir reconstructs a conversation from thirty years earlier. What is the best response?
choices: Use it critically as evidence while distinguishing recollection from exact transcript.
Treat every sentence as recorded verbatim.

activities.prompt: What follows if the plain-speaking persona is rhetorical?
choices: Nothing the speaker says can be true.
Style alone cannot guarantee sincerity; assess the claims and evidence.

activities.prompt: What is the safest conclusion about this passage?
choices: It shows how Plato presents Socrates’ preferred standard of judgment.
It proves every trial speech was identical.
It tells us every juror’s motive.

activities.prompt: Does uncertainty about exact speech make argument analysis impossible?
choices: No: we can analyze the argument in the surviving text.

activities.prompt: Explain why a primary source may be valuable without being a verbatim or neutral record. Apply the distinction to this passage.
activities.context: For I am more than seventy years of age, and appearing now for the first time in a court of law, I am quite a stranger to the language of the place; and therefore I would have you regard me as if I were really a stranger, whom you would excuse if he spoke in his native tongue, and after the fashion of his country:—Am I making an unfair request of you? Never mind the manner, which may or may not be good; but think only of the truth of my words, and give heed to that: let the speaker speak truly and the judge decide justly.
rubric: I identify Plato as the author and Socrates as the portrayed speaker.
I distinguish textual claims from historical reconstruction.
I explain a legitimate use of the source despite its limits.
